The charge solve: what A is, and what NNLS does with it

wft forward-fit reconstruction · every figure generated from sat_det3 (mx17_3, Saturday long run, resistive 490 V / drift 1000 V) with calib_bundle_r06, the corrected sharing kernel · 2026-08-21

A is a dictionary of pictures. Column k of A is the complete (strip × sample) picture that one unit of charge, liberated at drift depth k, would have produced in this window — geometry, charge sharing and amplifier response all folded in. There are 18 such pictures, one per 60 ns slice of the drift gap. Solving for q asks a single question: how much of each picture do I add up to reproduce what the detector actually recorded? Because that question is linear, it has an exact answer, and the fit never has to search for the charges — only for the three geometric numbers that decide which 18 pictures to draw.

1 · The problem, stated honestly

One plane of one event is an array of numbers: every strip in the window, every 60 ns sample. For the event this note follows, that is 17 strips × 32 samples = 544 numbers. Nothing has been reduced, thresholded or turned into a "hit" — this is the raw, pedestal- and gain-corrected window.

The physical picture behind those numbers: a charged particle crossed the 30 mm drift gap, ionising along its path. That ionisation drifts down to the mesh at v ≈ 36.6 µm/ns, so charge liberated deep in the gap arrives late. If the track is inclined, deep charge also arrives at a different transverse position. Every strip therefore sees a superposition of contributions from many drift depths, blurred by diffusion, spread onto its neighbours by the resistive layer, and finally shaped by the amplifier.

So the unknowns are:

unknownhow manyhow it enters the model how it is found
p₀ position at the mesh1 non-linearlysearched — Nelder-Mead, ~500 steps
w transverse speed (the slope)1 non-linearly
t₀ when the mesh charge arrives1 non-linearly
q₀ … q₁₇ charge per 60 ns depth slice 18linearly solved in closed form

That last row is the whole trick. Twenty-one unknowns would be a miserable search. But the model is linear in the charges: doubling the charge in a depth slice exactly doubles its contribution to every sample of every strip. Anything linear can be solved rather than searched.

The two-level structure. The expensive object — A — depends only on the three geometric numbers and the calibration. Given A, the charges come out of a closed-form solve, and the χ² that comes back is what the outer search actually navigates by.

2 · One column of A, built from scratch

Forget the matrix for a moment and ask a smaller question: if exactly one unit of charge were liberated at depth slice k, and nothing else happened, what would this window look like?

Answering it takes three ingredients, and they multiply:

  1. Where it lands. Slice k's charge sits at transverse position p₀ + w·uk, spread by a Gaussian whose width is the initial cloud, plus diffusion √u, plus the sideways motion of the track within the slice itself. Integrating that Gaussian across each 0.78 mm strip gives F[i,k] — the fraction landing on strip i. That is strip_fractions(), and it is pure geometry.
  2. When it arrives. The charge reaches the mesh at t₀ + uk, and the amplifier turns that instant into the measured pulse shape h(t). Sampling h(t − t₀ − uk) at the 32 sample times gives H0[:,k].
  3. Who else sees it. The resistive layer puts a fraction c₁ of a strip's charge onto each ±1 neighbour and c₂ onto each ±2, with their own, slightly later, response shapes h₁ and h₂.
columnk = F:,k ⊗ hk  +  c₁ · F±1:,k ⊗ h₁,k  +  c₂ · F±2:,k ⊗ h₂,k ⊗ is an outer product: a vector over strips times a vector over samples gives a strip × sample picture. Three of them, added.

Do that for all eighteen depth slices and you have the whole of A. Seen side by side, the columns tell you what the fit is actually able to distinguish:

3 · Why it is a matrix at all: the flattening

Each column is naturally a 2-D picture, 17 × 32. Linear algebra wants vectors, so the picture is unrolled row by row: strip 0's 32 samples, then strip 1's 32 samples, and so on. Row index r = i·32 + s. That is the single line M.reshape(n·NSAMP, K) at the end of build_matrix, and it is the only thing standing between "a stack of pictures" and "a matrix".

The one-line summary. A is tall and thin: 544 rows (one per measurement) by 18 columns (one per unknown charge). Tall and thin is good — it means the problem is over-determined by a factor of thirty, which is why an 18-number answer extracted from a noisy window is stable at all.

4 · The equation being solved

Sections 2 and 3 built A from the bottom up, one column at a time. It is worth stopping to write down the equation those columns are a discretisation of — because everything the fit can and cannot do follows from its structure, and because that structure is clearest in one dimension, where the same equation collapses to a textbook problem with a textbook pathology.

4.1 The equation, in full

A track crossing the gap liberates charge along its path. Label that charge not by where it was born but by when it arrives at the mesh: let λ(u) du be the charge reaching the mesh between u and u + du after t₀, the arrival time of the shallowest charge. Depth and arrival time are the same coordinate — z = v·u, with v = 36.6 µm/ns, so one 60 ns slice is 2.2 mm of gap — and λ(u) is the only thing about the ionisation the detector can report.

Charge in slice u lands at transverse position p₀ + w·u, spread by a Gaussian, and strip i collects whatever falls inside its pitch:

Si(u) = ∫xi − P/2xi + P/2 dp   N( p ; p₀ + w·u , σ(u) ) σ²(u) = σ₀² + Dp²·u + (w·Δu)²/12 — the initial cloud, the diffusion accumulated over the drift, and the track's own sideways travel inside one 60 ns slice. P = 0.78 mm is the strip pitch. This integral is strip_fractions(), and it is the whole of the transverse physics.

Each strip's charge then rings the amplifier, and a fraction of it appears on the neighbours through the resistive layer. Put together, the equation the reconstruction is trying to solve is:

yi(t) = ∫0∞ du   λ(u)  [  Si(u)·h(t − t₀ − u)  +  c₁·(Si−1 + Si+1)(u)·h₁(t − t₀ − u)  +  c₂·(Si−2 + Si+2)(u)·h₂(t − t₀ − u)  ]  + εi(t) yi(t): the gain-corrected waveform on strip i. h: the measured impulse response; h₁ and h₂ its RC-dispersed copies on the ±1 and ±2 neighbours, with amplitudes c₁ and c₂. ε: the per-strip noise. Unknown: the function λ(u) ≥ 0, and the three numbers p₀, w, t₀ buried inside the kernel.

That is a Fredholm integral equation of the first kind — a measured left-hand side, a known kernel, an unknown non-negative function under the integral — with the extra twist that three parameters of the kernel are unknown as well. Everything in this note is one particular way of attacking it: discretise λ, solve for it exactly, search the three.

What the equation quietly assumes.
  • One track. Two tracks in one window need two copies of the whole bracket, each with its own p₀, w and its own λ. Clusters more than 12 mm apart get separate windows and are fitted separately; a genuinely merged pair would need a 2K-column matrix and is the one tier of the multi-track generalisation that is not built (wft/MULTITRACK_2026-08-12.md) — such events show up as one compromise track with a large χ²/dof.
  • One plane at a time. x and y are fitted independently, each with its own λ; nothing in the equation forces the two profiles to agree.
  • λ ≥ 0. Charge, not signal — the constraint that makes §8 necessary.
  • A calibrated, position-independent response. h, c₁, c₂, σ₀ and Dp come from the bundle and are the same everywhere on the detector; per-channel gain is divided out of y before the fit, not carried in the kernel.

4.2 Discretising it: where A comes from

Two discretisations turn that integral into arithmetic. The waveform is sampled — t → ts, 32 of them, 60 ns apart. And λ is taken constant across each 60 ns slice of drift — λ(u) → qk, K = 18 of them. The integral becomes a sum, and the bracket evaluated at uk is column k:

y = A(p₀, w, t₀)·q + ε ,   q ≥ 0 with A[(i,s), k] = the bracket above, at strip i, sample ts, slice uk. That is build_matrix, and Figures 2–4 are its three factors, one column, and the flattening.

Strip the noise off and that is an ordinary system of linear equations — A q = y, matrix times column vector — with one equation per measurement:

for every strip i and sample s:   Σk A[(i,s), k] · qk = yi(s) A is 544 × 18, q is 18 × 1, y is 544 × 1. In words: the eighteen pictures, scaled by their charges, add up to what the detector recorded.

Two things about that system decide everything that follows. It is overdetermined — 544 equations for 18 unknowns — so with noise in y there is no q satisfying all of them, and A, not being square, has no inverse to apply. "Solve" therefore means miss by the least: take the q that minimises ‖A q − y‖². Setting the derivative to zero gives Aᵀ(A q − y) = 0, the normal equations AᵀA·q = Aᵀ·y, and only then q̂ = (AᵀA)−1Aᵀy. The matrix that gets inverted is never A: it is the 18 × 18 AᵀA, the table of overlaps between columns. §4.5 does that arithmetic on a 12 × 2 example, §6 is the same statement as a picture, and §7 is what changes when q ≥ 0 is enforced — the production code calls scipy.optimize.nnls and never forms the inverse at all.

λ(u)the NNLS answer q18
Si(u)strip_fractions() → F 17 × 18
h, h₁, h₂_time_tensors() → H0, H1, H2 32 × 18
p₀, w, t₀the Nelder-Mead vector3
εiper-strip noise → the row weights §5

4.3 The same equation in one dimension

Now delete a dimension. Sum the equation over strips: the S's sum to one — all the charge lands on some strip, bar the tails that fall off the ends of the window — and the two neighbour terms sum to twice that, so the strip index vanishes entirely and what is left is

Y(t) = ∫ du   λ(u)·g(t − t₀ − u)  =  (λ ∗ g)(t − t₀) ,    g = h + 2c₁h₁ + 2c₂h₂ A plain convolution. Discretised, Y = H·q with H a Toeplitz matrix of shifted copies of g — the classic one-dimensional deconvolution.

This is not a thought experiment: it is this event, with only the information about which strip saw the charge thrown away.

The pathology is entirely in the numbers. The impulse response is 300 ns wide at half maximum — five depth bins — so consecutive columns of H are nearly the same picture, correlated at 0.955. The matrix is ill-conditioned (cond = 3,381), and the price is paid in the answer: the unconstrained error on one bin's charge is 5,928 on an event whose total charge is only 5,672. In one dimension a single depth bin is not measured at all.

What is measured in 1-D is everything smooth. The error on the total charge is 42, i.e. 0.7 % — the arrival time and the amount of charge are fine; only the fine structure is destroyed. That is the standard behaviour of a first-kind integral equation, and the standard responses to it are regularisation — a smoothness or entropy penalty, or a parametric shape for λ. None of those is used here. Non-negativity does some of that work (§8), but the real answer is different: put the missing dimension back.

4.4 Back up to our dimensionality, one dimension at a time

Step 1 — restore the strips, but keep the track vertical. Set w = 0: every depth slice now lands on a strip pattern, but on the same pattern, wider with depth only through diffusion. The problem grows from 32 rows to 544, and almost none of that is new information about depth: the condition number moves from 3,381 to 3,273. The per-bin error does improve, 5,928 → 2,353, but that is just the noise averaging down over 17 strips. Seventeen times the data, the same degeneracy.

Step 2 — let the track lean. With w ≠ 0, slice k lands at p₀ + w·uk — a different place for every k, and the place and the time are locked to each other by the single number w. Now the columns are distinguishable by something other than a time shift the response has already smeared over, and the problem transforms: cond 3,273 → 91, per-bin error 2,353 → 77. A factor of thirty in charge resolution, bought from geometry — not from better electronics, a finer clock or a lower noise floor.

problemrowscond(A) σ of one binσ of the total
1-D — strips summed away32 3,3815,928 42
17 strips, vertical track (w = 0) 5443,273 2,35311
17 strips, this track (w = 0.0088 mm/ns, tan θ = 0.24) 54491 7714

Unconstrained errors, all 18 bins, noise-weighted units. The q ≥ 0 constraint switches most bins off and shrinks the error bars on the survivors — §10 and Figure 14 quote those instead.

The strips are not there for statistics. They are there to break the depth degeneracy — and they only do it when the track leans. Two consequences follow. The angle is not a by-product of the charge profile; it is the parameter that makes the charge profile measurable, which is why the χ² is sharp in w. And a near-vertical track is intrinsically the hard case: its depth profile is barely determined, whatever the electronics do.

Step 3 — put the neighbours back. Charge sharing adds no unknowns at all; it adds the c₁ and c₂ terms inside the bracket. It makes the transverse handle slightly blunter — sharing correlates strips that geometry had separated, which is exactly why the kernel's ordering has to be right (c₂ < c₁, always) — but because it lives in A rather than in the data, it biases nothing. That is the point §13 makes at length, and the reason this basis exists at all.

Step 4 — flatten, weight, censor. §3 unrolled the pictures into columns; §5 divides every row by its strip's noise and drops the rows that are saturated or dead. What is left is the finite problem the code actually solves:

minimise over (p₀, w, t₀)  of  [  minimise over q ≥ 0  of  ‖ ( y − A(p₀, w, t₀)·q ) / σ ‖²  ] 544 numbers in; 18 charges solved exactly in the inner bracket, 3 geometric numbers searched in the outer one. The inner solve is §6–§8; the outer search is §11.

4.5 A worked example small enough to check by hand

The real problem is 544 × 18. The structure is identical at 12 × 2, so here is one built from scratch: 3 strips, 4 samples, 2 depth slices. The "template" is h = [0, 1, 0.5, 0.1]; slice 0 lands 20/60/20 % across the three strips and slice 1, being deeper on an inclined track, lands 5/35/60 %. The true charges are 100 and 60, and Gaussian noise of σ = 2 is added.

The arithmetic in the right-hand panel is the entire "solve" step:

q̂ = (AᵀA)−1 Aᵀy AᵀA is 2 × 2 here and 18 × 18 in the real problem — never 544 × 544. That is why this is fast.

AᵀA is the matrix of overlaps between columns: entry (k, k′) is how much picture k looks like picture k′. Aᵀy is the matrix of overlaps between each column and the data — "how much does the data resemble depth slice k?". The solve trades one against the other: a bin gets credit for the data it matches, minus what its neighbours have already explained. In the toy the two columns overlap at 0.736, which is almost exactly the 0.80 that adjacent depth bins overlap at in the real matrix — the toy is not a caricature, it is the same problem with the indices turned down.

5 · What the fit is allowed to look at: weights and censoring

Two adjustments happen before the solve, and both are edits to A and y rather than to the model.

Noise weighting

χ² compares residuals to the noise, so every row is divided by that strip's own σ: A ← A/σ, y ← y/σ. After that division the residual in every row has unit variance and the plain sum of squares is the χ². On det3 the strips are uniform (σ ≈ 7.4 ADC) so this barely changes the answer — its purpose is the cases where the strips are not uniform, and the dead-channel case below, where it is doing the real work.

Censoring

Two kinds of row carry no usable information and are deleted from A entirely:

  • Saturated samples. Above 3550 ADC the amplifier clips; the sample says "at least this much" and nothing more. Those rows leave the fit, and are replaced by a one-sided penalty that fires only if the model falls below the clipped value.
  • Dead channels. A broken connection reads baseline, not zero charge. Those rows are censored the same way and their σ is set to 10⁹ so the one-sided penalty cannot pull on them either — no information in either direction. (This is the machinery that masks chamber A's connector 8 on run_79.)

6 · The solve, geometrically

With A and y fixed, "fit the charges" means: find the combination of columns that comes closest to the data vector. The set of all reachable combinations, {Aq}, is a flat 18-dimensional subspace inside 544-dimensional space — the column space. Least squares picks the point of that subspace nearest to y, and the nearest point is found by dropping a perpendicular.

The picture behind (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀy. The residual is perpendicular to every column of A — that perpendicularity, written out, is the normal equations. The data will never lie exactly in the column space; noise and model imperfection are precisely the part of y that no charge profile can reach.

…and then non-negativity bends it

Charge cannot be negative. That single constraint changes the character of the answer completely, and it is worth seeing why on real columns.

7 · How the constrained solve actually runs

scipy.optimize.nnls is the Lawson–Hanson active-set algorithm. It is not iterative refinement and it does not "converge" in the usual sense: it terminates in a finite number of steps at the exact constrained optimum. The recipe is short enough to state in full:

start with every charge at zero and every constraint ACTIVE
loop:
    gradient = Aᵀ(y − Aq)          "which bin most wants charge?"
    if no active bin has a positive gradient: STOP — this is the optimum
    move that bin into the FREE set
    solve the ordinary least-squares problem on the free set alone
    while any freed charge came out negative:
        back off along the line to the constraint boundary,
        re-activate whatever hit zero, and re-solve

Instrumenting it on the display event shows the whole story. (The instrumented implementation reproduces scipy's answer to 4e-12 — it is the same algorithm, only narrating.)

Two things in that figure are worth dwelling on. The order of admission is not depth order — it is 10, 1, 6, 13, 3, 0, 7, 12, 5, 2, 4, 6 — because each step picks whichever depth best explains what is left over. And the first step alone removes 45 % of the χ²: one depth slice, chosen greedily, is already most of the answer.

The display event never backtracks; most events do. Over 250 planes, 91 % need at least one bin pushed back out of the free set, and one needed 26. The backtracking loop is not decoration — it is what makes the answer exact rather than greedy.

8 · Why non-negativity is not cosmetic

It is tempting to think the constraint is a tidy-up. It is not: without it the solve produces a profile that fits marginally better and means nothing.

The negative excursions are physically impossible and they cancel almost perfectly, which is exactly why the χ² hardly notices them. Everything downstream that uses the profile — the charge column endpoint that measures the drift gap, the arrival quantiles, the candidate score — would be reading noise. The 27 % of χ² given up by forbidding them is the price of an interpretable answer, and it is a bargain.

9 · How independent are the eighteen unknowns, really?

The zeros in a charge profile look alarming until you look at how much the columns of A resemble each other. Adjacent depth slices are separated by 60 ns of drift — but the amplifier response is hundreds of nanoseconds wide, so their pictures overlap heavily.

This is the single most useful thing to understand about q. The data constrains smooth functionals of the charge profile extremely well and bin-to-bin structure hardly at all. So: the total charge, the median arrival time, the depth at which the column ends — trustworthy. The value of one individual bin, or the pattern of which bins happen to be zero — not a measurement. The pipeline is built accordingly: what fit_plane keeps from q is exactly q_sum, q_u50, q_u90 and q_uend — four smooth summaries, not the eighteen numbers.

10 · The answer, and its error bars

Errors on the charges come from the same matrix, restricted to the bins that survived: cov = (Afreeᵀ Afree)⁻¹. The contrast between a single bin and a smooth summary is stark.

Note the numbers: a single bin is known to a few per cent at best, while their sum is known to 0.22 %. That factor is the anti-correlation doing its work, and it is the quantitative version of the warning in §9.

11 · Why this is called "profiling", and what the outer loop sees

The charges are nuisance parameters. They are not thrown away and they are not guessed once and held: they are re-derived exactly at every single trial geometry. What the outer search navigates by is the χ² after that re-derivation — a profile likelihood in the statistical sense.

The middle panel is also the clearest picture of why the fit works at all. A wrong p₀ can still be made to fit the data — but only by an unphysical, lumpy charge profile. The geometry is determined not because a wrong geometry cannot describe the waveforms, but because it can only do so by demanding an absurd distribution of ionisation.

The degeneracy this leaves behind

There is one direction in which the trade is nearly free. Shift t₀ earlier by one depth bin and slide p₀ along the track by w·60 ns, and the charge profile simply moves one index over — the model waveforms are almost unchanged.

This is why the scintillator t₀ prior exists. A free fit lands in the physically correct tooth only about a third of the time. The trigger, through the ftst clock phase, predicts t₀ per event to a few nanoseconds; a Gaussian penalty on that prediction (σ = 5 ns, carried in the bundle as t0_abs / t0_prior_sigma) is what selects the right one. It was A/B-validated on held-out data on 2026-08-12 and is the production configuration on the bench. It is bench-only — t0_abs must be dropped when a bundle is transferred to beam running, where there is no such trigger.

12 · What this looks like across a population

The median trap, which has already cost us once. Summarising these profiles with a per-bin median made the drift column read 24.7 mm and launched a hunt for a "missing 4 mm of gap". Means, trimmed means or rebinned medians moved it to 27.9 mm and the hardware question evaporated. Anything that summarises a sparse NNLS profile must account for the sparsity — the zeros are constraint boundaries, not measurements of "no charge here".

The first-bin spike in the right-hand panel is real and worth knowing about: bin 0 is where anything arriving earlier than the model expects gets deposited, so it absorbs t₀ mismatch. It is another reason to read the column endpoint rather than the first bin.

13 · The neighbours are in A, not in the way

One structural point deserves its own section, because it is the reason this whole approach exists. On a resistive-strip detector each strip's signal contains delayed, dispersed copies of its neighbours'. If you reduce a strip to a single hit time, that contamination is irreducible — it compresses the drift-time ladder by 20–30 % and reads the angle several degrees too steep, and no threshold or estimator change fixes it.

Here, the copies are terms in the model. They are part of what a unit of charge is predicted to look like, so the solve accounts for them instead of being fooled by them.

14 · Traps

  • The stored c2 is 0.0, and it is not zero. The ±2 amplitude is slaved to the ±1 one (c2 = 0.6 · c1), so the stored c2 field is literally 0.0 and the ratio lives in the c2_over_c1 hyper. Code that reads h['c2'] directly draws no ±2 copy at all and builds a subtly wrong A. Use wft.calib.effective_c2(), build_matrix, or bundle.summary(), all of which report what the model actually uses. Figure 16 of this note walked straight into it on the day the note was written, which is why the trap is first in the list.
  • c₂ > c₁ is a defect, and it no longer loads. Until 2026-08-21 every shipped bundle carried a ±2 copy larger than the ±1 copy — det3 1.14, det2 1.53, det7 1.75, det4 2.12 — which cannot be physical, since the ±2 strip is reached only through the ±1. It is not a measurement but an artefact of a genuinely flat χ² direction, which an unconstrained fit walks along; the H4 head-on beam measures the ratio model-free at 0.45 ± 0.02. wft.calib.check_kernel_ordering() now refuses such a bundle at load, at save and at install, so no analysis can pick one up by accident. Every product built on one has been retired and re-reconstructed on the corrected kernel.
  • K is not universal. 18 bins of 60 ns is a det3-at-1000-V number. Slower chambers need 22 or 26 bins or the charge column runs off the end of the basis, and the fit then piles charge into the last bin and biases t₀.
  • t₀ is quantised to 5 ns during the coarse searches. Building A is the expensive step and it depends on t₀ but not on p₀ or w, so the three time tensors are cached on a 5 ns grid. The final Nelder-Mead steps run unsnapped and pay full price. If you call build_matrix yourself with an off-grid t₀ you take the slow path — which is correct, just slower.
  • σp0 absorbs model error. If the sharing kernel is wrong, the fit can hide the missing transverse spread by inflating the "initial cloud" instead. A σp0 of half a millimetre is not a measurement of the primary ionisation cloud, it is a warning light.

15 · Reproduce

cd docs/charge_solve
../../.venv/bin/python figs.py        # 18 figures + numbers.json, ~50 s
../../.venv/bin/python make_note.py   # this page

# override the inputs:
#   WFT_DOC_BUNDLE=<path to a calib bundle>   CS_FIGDIR=<where the PNGs go>

Everything is driven by the live products under <Analysis>/mx17_det3_saturday_scan_6-27-26/long_run_resist_490V_drift_1000V/mx17_3/wft/: the bundle calib_bundle_r06 and the 400-event ref-pinned calibration cache. The code under discussion is wft/model.py — build_matrix(), strip_fractions() and chi2_plane() are the three functions this whole note is about, and together they are about eighty lines.

Companion reading: the full nine-part reference document docs/wft_reference/ covers the rest of the chain, from raw ADC to physics outputs; RECONSTRUCTION_BASIS.md is why geometry comes from waveforms and never from hit times.
